notes.meaning: Jacob traveled to Beersheba, the southern border of Canaan, and offered sacrifices to God. Abraham and Isaac had also built altars and worshiped God in that place. Jacob paused to thank the Lord and ask for His guidance before leaving the land God had promised to his family.

God spoke to Jacob in a night vision and called him by name twice. Repeating Jacob's name showed God's personal care and called for his close attention. Jacob answered right away, showing he was ready to listen and follow God's direction.

God introduced Himself as the God of Jacob's father Isaac and told him not to be afraid of moving to Egypt. Jacob may have worried about leaving the promised land, facing Egyptian idolatry, or moving his large family in his old age. God comforted him with the promise that his family would grow into a great nation while living there.

God promised to go with Jacob down to Egypt and bring his people back to Canaan in the future. This promise looked ahead both to Jacob's body being brought back for burial and to the entire nation returning hundreds of years later. God also gave him the tender comfort that his beloved son Joseph would be at his side to close his eyes when he died.

Encouraged by God's promise, Jacob set out from Beersheba with renewed energy. His sons placed their elderly father, their children, and their wives into the wagons Pharaoh had provided. Jacob was too weak from old age to make the long trek on foot, so his family cared for him along the road.

Jacob's family gathered their livestock and the belongings they had earned in Canaan and set out for Egypt. Jacob brought all his sons, grandsons, daughters, and granddaughters with him, leaving no one behind. Moving the whole household showed their complete trust that God was leading them into this new chapter.

This passage introduces the formal family record of the Israelites who went down to Egypt. Reuben is named first because he was Jacob's firstborn son. Even though Reuben had lost his privileges as the oldest because of his past sin, he was still listed first in the family order.

These verses name the sons of Reuben, Simeon, and Levi. Each of these sons grew into a family leader and became the founder of an Israelite clan. Levi's three sons—Gershon, Kohath, and Merari—became the heads of the main divisions of Israel's future priestly tribe.

Judah's family is listed next, along with a reminder that his first two sons, Er and Onan, had already died in Canaan. Perez had two sons named Hezron and Hamul, who were counted in the family line to take their place. Judah's line was especially significant because it would lead to King David and ultimately to Jesus Christ.

Issachar had four sons, and Zebulun had three sons. These men would all become heads of clans within their respective tribes. Their households grew rapidly in Egypt, fulfilling God's ancient promise to multiply the family of Abraham.

Here the family record summarizes the line of Jacob born through his wife Leah, including his daughter Dinah. The total number for this group is given as thirty-three people. The count reaches thirty-three when Jacob himself is included alongside Leah's children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren.

These verses list the descendants of Zilpah, the maidservant whom Laban had given to Leah. Her sons Gad and Asher had many children, and Asher had a notable daughter named Serah. Zilpah's branch of the family totaled sixteen people who entered Egypt.

Rachel is singled out as Jacob's chosen wife, and her two sons were Joseph and Benjamin. Joseph's two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, were born in Egypt to his Egyptian wife Asenath before Jacob arrived. They are listed here because they would later become two distinct tribes in the nation of Israel.

Benjamin is listed with ten sons, making his household remarkably large. Several of these names were likely Benjamin's grandsons who were counted directly under him as clan heads. Rachel's entire family line, including Joseph, Benjamin, and their descendants, totaled fourteen people.

These verses record the descendants born through Bilhah, the maidservant given to Rachel. Dan had one son named Hushim, while Naphtali had four sons. In all, Bilhah's branch added seven people to the family traveling to Egypt.

The family members who traveled directly with Jacob to Egypt numbered sixty-six, not counting his sons' wives. Adding Jacob himself, along with Joseph and his two sons already living in Egypt, brought the entire family of Israel to seventy people. God kept track of this exact number to show how He later multiplied a small, seventy-person family into a massive nation.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars note that the Greek translation of the Old Testament added five descendants of Joseph to reach seventy-five people, which is the number Stephen quoted in Acts 7:14.

notes.meaning: Jacob sent Judah ahead of the caravan to meet Joseph and get directions to the region of Goshen. Judah had proved himself to be a trustworthy, caring leader when he spoke up for Benjamin back in Egypt. His leadership helped the entire family journey smoothly into their new homeland.

Joseph prepared his royal chariot and rode out to Goshen to meet his father. When they saw each other, Joseph threw his arms around Jacob's neck and wept for a long time. Their tearful reunion was full of joy and relief after more than twenty years of painful separation.

Jacob told Joseph that he was now ready to die in peace since he had seen his son's face and knew he was still alive. His deepest sorrow had turned to comfort, and his greatest earthly desire was granted. He was content to leave this world whenever God called him, knowing God had been faithful to him.

Joseph told his family that he would go before Pharaoh to announce their arrival. He planned to tell the king plainly that his brothers were shepherds who had brought all their flocks and herds. Joseph was not embarrassed by his family's humble trade and wanted Pharaoh to understand their way of life from the start.

Joseph instructed his brothers to tell Pharaoh honestly that their family had raised livestock for generations. He wanted them to settle in Goshen, a fertile pasture land away from the main Egyptian cities. Because native Egyptians looked down on shepherds, living apart in Goshen protected Israel from adopting Egyptian customs and allowed them to grow as a separate people.
